# ABHEDYA Product Requirements Document

Version: 1.0 · Status: Draft derived from the frozen ABHEDYA v2 instruction pack
Project: TM005136 · SFIC 2026 · PS0001 · Secure, Isolated and Auditable Cybersecurity Testing Platform
Scope authority: `docs/03_CONTEXT.md`, `docs/04_CONTRACTS.md`, `docs/05_OBJECTIVES.md`, and the machine-readable contracts in `contracts/`.
This PRD describes the product the team intends to build; it is not evidence that the implementation exists or has passed its tests.
Contract precedence: `contracts/schema.sql`, `contracts/rbac_matrix.yaml`, and `contracts/audit_vectors.json` are authoritative; conflicts require an agreed change request.
Line-count policy: written in 6 full 800-line append chunks plus a final 646-line remainder; chunk markers identify the actual append batches.

## 1. Product summary

ABHEDYA is a laptop-scale cyber testing platform for multiple teams that need separate places to test applications, suspicious files, and AI systems.
A user creates or submits a workload through a browser console; an API records desired state; a runner reconciles that state into constrained containers.
The platform uses gVisor `runsc` for the planned sandbox tier and must make any degraded isolation tier visible to users and auditors.
A PostgreSQL database stores identity, tenant ownership, workload state, jobs, metrics, activity events, audit records, and checkpoints.
A notary signs checkpoint roots; an independent command-line verifier checks exported records without importing the platform implementation.
The product is designed for a single demo host, offline operation after setup, and an outside jury member who can inspect evidence.
It is not a general-purpose cloud, enterprise SIEM, production malware-analysis service, or guarantee that a file marked clean is safe.

## 2. Product outcomes and success definition

Success is measured by the named tests in `docs/06_VERIFICATION.md`, not by visual polish or an unverified claim.
Each objective O1–O9 is complete only when all of its listed tests pass on the demo host and the required evidence file exists.
The demo should let a reviewer observe one successful workflow and then attempt representative boundary violations themselves.
The product must run without internet access at the venue after images, dependencies, probe sets, rules and certificates are prepared.
A failure or degraded mode must be visible in the console, activity stream or audit record; a silent fallback is a product defect.
The product must not label a file verdict `clean` as a safety guarantee or describe AI scanner output as ground truth.

## 3. User groups and product responsibilities

### 3.1 Analyst
An analyst belongs to exactly one team and uses environments and jobs within the ownership rules in the RBAC matrix.
An analyst may create an app-target environment, submit a file, start an AI scan, and inspect only their own job output where the matrix says `own`.
An analyst must receive a 404 for another team's object and a 403 for a teammate's object when a rule is scoped to `own`.
An analyst must not receive audit events through the live stream, even when those events concern the analyst's own team.
### 3.2 Team lead
A team lead is scoped to one team and can manage team-scoped work under the matrix.
A team lead may review their team's environments, events, jobs and audit view only where their specific rule allows it.
A team lead may stop or destroy team environments and may create workloads subject to quota admission.
A team lead cannot read another team's records or change platform-wide users and teams.
### 3.3 Administrator
An administrator is a platform role without a team association.
An administrator can manage users, teams, quotas, overview and kill-switch actions as defined by the matrix.
An administrator can stop or destroy environments, but deliberately cannot execute commands in sandboxes or read team job output.
An administrator's mutation and refusal outcomes must be attributable in the audit ledger.
### 3.4 Auditor
An auditor is a platform role without a team association and has read-oriented platform oversight.
An auditor can inspect and export audit data, verify the ledger and view platform overview as allowed by the matrix.
An auditor cannot execute tenant workloads or read team job output, preserving the confidentiality rule in R17–R21.
### 3.5 Outside reviewer or jury member
The reviewer can run the standalone verifier using an exported ledger, public key and witness file.
The reviewer should be able to choose a record and field for a tamper drill and see the exact verifier verdict.
The reviewer is not required to trust the application UI as the sole proof of audit integrity.

## 4. Product boundaries

Included: role-based browser access, environment lifecycle, three workload types, quotas, real-time monitoring, audit verification, admin oversight and evidence export.
Included: per-team ownership on application objects and server-side filtering before data reaches a browser stream.
Included: single-host operation with one Docker daemon and one active runner stack under the demo-host operating rules.
Excluded from mandatory scope: multi-host scheduling, high availability, production customer data, Windows malware detonation and GPU-hosted inference.
Excluded from mandatory scope: TOTP, interactive browser terminal, external checkpoint anchoring, in-browser verification, runtime syscall telemetry, ClamAV, inclusion proofs and a real local model; these are stretch items S1–S8.
Excluded from product claims: absolute sandbox security, hardware side-channel resistance, certainty of static/dynamic file verdicts, or certainty of AI scan findings.

## 5. Product-wide experience requirements

All application routes use `/api/v1`; the browser communicates over HTTPS through the edge proxy.
Every API response exposes an `X-Request-ID`; mutation audit entries use that same request ID.
API errors use the closed error-code list and the documented JSON envelope; the UI should show a human-readable message and preserve the request ID for support.
The UI must not render user-supplied command text, filenames or job output as executable HTML.
The UI must display workload state as desired state and observed state separately when the runner is reconciling.
The UI must display the isolation tier and a warning when the runtime is degraded or not `gvisor`.
The UI must show fixed resource limits derived from S, M or L; users do not submit arbitrary CPU, memory, storage or PID values.
List views use pagination limits from 1 to 200 and must not return rows outside the caller's scope.
Audit and activity views distinguish informational, warning and critical severity without claiming that severity itself proves an incident.

## 7. Workload product requirements

### 7.1 Application target

The `app-target` template consists of a vulnerable target and a toolbox in the same environment-specific network.
The toolbox can reach the target by its environment-local service name, as verified by T-WL-01.
A toolbox in another environment must not resolve that target name or reach its IP address.
The console submits a command to R17 as a job; it does not execute user text in a host shell.
Command input is 1–4096 characters; the optional container value is `toolbox` or `target`, defaulting to `toolbox`.
Command output combines stdout and stderr, is limited to 65,536 bytes, and records whether output was truncated.
An exec job times out after 60 seconds and reports status `timeout`.
The environment must be in observed state `running` before R17 accepts execution; otherwise return 409 `ENV_NOT_RUNNING` and audit the denial.
### 7.2 File analysis

R20 accepts a multipart file of at most 10 MiB and a Boolean `detonate` option.
The product computes SHA-256 and stores bytes under the quarantine directory using the digest, never the uploaded filename.
The quarantined file has mode 0400 and is never executed outside a sandbox.
Static triage reports file type and YARA matches; the exact result uses the schema in `docs/04_CONTRACTS.md`.
Optional detonation runs without a network interface other than loopback and is time-limited to 120 seconds.
A malicious-tagged YARA match yields `malicious`; another match or timed-out detonation yields `suspicious`; no match yields `clean`; pipeline error yields `unknown`.
The UI must show the rule name and explain that a clean result is not proof of safety.
After a file job ends, its environment resources must be removed; T-WL-02 checks for remaining labeled containers, networks and volumes.
### 7.3 AI red-team scan

R21 accepts target `stub-vulnerable` or `stub-guarded` and probe set `quick` or `full`.
The scan runs garak probes against the offline stub service; it does not require a production model or internet access.
Each finding identifies a probe, attempts, failures and an OWASP LLM risk ID.
The result includes total attempts, total failures and a SHA-256 report digest.
The demo acceptance compares vulnerable and guarded target behavior; the guarded target must have strictly fewer failures.
The UI labels outcomes `scanner-flagged` and must not present an absolute risk score as ground truth.
The AI environment is size M and TTL 10 minutes under the product resource policy.

## 8. Environment lifecycle and resource experience

An analyst or team lead requests an environment using a unique team-local name, a supported template and S, M or L size.
The API creates a row with desired state `running` and observed state `requested`; the runner later moves through provisioning to running or failed.
The console presents transitions and failure reasons; a request accepted by the API is not mislabeled as a running sandbox.
Default TTL is 60 minutes and maximum user-selected TTL is 240 minutes; file and AI environments use 10 minutes.
Size S maps to 500 CPU millis, 256 MiB memory, 128 MiB storage and 128 PIDs.
Size M maps to 1000 CPU millis, 512 MiB memory, 256 MiB storage and 256 PIDs.
Size L maps to 2000 CPU millis, 1024 MiB memory, 512 MiB storage and 512 PIDs.
Quota admission includes active/requested/provisioning environments except observed `destroyed` or `failed` environments.
Admission checks team quota and host reserved capacity in the same transaction as environment insertion.
A quota refusal is 409 `QUOTA_EXCEEDED`, produces no environment, and is recorded as denied.
Stopping and destroying are asynchronous desired-state requests; the console waits for observed state instead of implying immediate destruction.
When TTL expires, the runner removes container, network and volume resources bearing the environment identifier.
The admin kill switch sets desired state to stopped for the requested team or for all teams when `team_id` is null.

## 9. Live monitoring requirements

The browser uses Server-Sent Events at R22; activity events carry IDs so Last-Event-ID can resume from the last received event.
Environment state change becomes visible within 3 seconds of the database change.
A running environment emits a metric sample at least every 5 seconds.
A tamper alert reaches the console within 30 seconds of detecting changed history.
Metrics show CPU percent relative to the environment limit, memory, storage, PID count and network byte counters.
A memory alert is raised above 90 percent of limit for three samples; CPU saturation above 95 percent for five samples; storage high above 90 percent.
An OOM kill appears as critical activity and the affected environment state is reconciled.
Team leads and analysts receive only in-scope activity; platform roles receive platform-wide activity only where their matrix allows.
Analysts receive no audit SSE records; the server filters events before serialization.
Disconnected clients may replay activity from Last-Event-ID; the product must not silently reorder or duplicate the ten-event recovery test.

## 10. Audit and trust requirements

A state-changing API operation and its audit record commit atomically; audit insert failure must roll back the state change.
Every listed mutation, failed login, scope denial and business-rule denial is recorded exactly once through `abh_core.audit.append`.
Anonymous 401 requests other than login do not write audit records; they may create rate-limited `authn.anonymous_rejected` activity.
The ledger body contains the exact 15 fields in the canonical contract and the record hash is unique.
The UI offers audit filtering, NDJSON export, public-key display and verification.
The verifier produces the contract verdict and sequence/tree size; the first failing condition wins per the verification algorithm.
Checkpoint signatures use Ed25519; the witness copy is outside the database but under the same operator, a known limit.
The platform states that records newer than the latest checkpoint can be truncated within the documented checkpoint window.
The product does not claim protection from a coordinated attacker controlling database, witness volume and signing key.

## 11. Privacy, safety and data handling

User responses never expose password hashes, TOTP secrets, lockout counters, raw session tokens or another user's CSRF token.
Job output is visible only to the caller's authorized team/ownership scope; platform admin and auditor cannot use R17–R21 to read tenant output.
Uploaded samples are addressed by digest rather than the original filename to avoid path interpretation and filename leakage.
Audit detail must avoid storing secrets, raw passwords, session tokens, signing keys or uploaded file bytes.
The browser treats command strings, filenames and job outputs as untrusted text.
The host and runner remain part of the trusted computing base; platform compromise is not represented as solved by the UI.

## 12. Acceptance method

Contract tests use the real schema and vectors; security tests use the real PostgreSQL, Docker and `runsc` on the demo VM.
No test in contract, security or end-to-end suites may be skipped, weakened, mocked or deleted to claim acceptance.
The evidence pack records versions, command outputs, test XML, scanner output, witness/export/verifier results and an outsider break-it session.
The demo walkthrough is seven minutes and includes a tenant-boundary attempt, resource exhaustion, file/AI jobs and jury-chosen audit tampering.
A product claim is permitted only when the associated test passes and its evidence artifact is present.

## 13. Route-specific product acceptance register
This register contains one role-independent anonymous case per API rule and separate authenticated cases by declared role.
The canonical RBAC matrix remains authoritative; each case tests a route result without creating a new permission.
### PRD-R01-ANONYMOUS
[PRD-R01-ANONYMOUS-D01] User need: `authenticate a named user` through `POST /auth/login`; actor=`anonymous (no authenticated role)`; authenticated RBAC scope=`none`.
[PRD-R01-ANONYMOUS-D02] Scenario procedure: Send `/auth/login` with no cookie; require 401 and no protected response body or state change.
[PRD-R01-ANONYMOUS-D03] Required product behavior: R01 is public login: valid credentials return the documented User, csrf_token and session cookie; failures use the same unknown-email/wrong-password response class and failed login attempts are audited as auth.login.
[PRD-R01-ANONYMOUS-D04] Evidence: T-RBAC-01 asserts the public unauthenticated rule; T-AUTH-01, T-AUTH-02, T-AUTH-03 and T-AUD-02 verify hashing, session response, indistinguishable failures and login audit.
### PRD-R01-ADMIN-AUTHORIZED-USE
[PRD-R01-ADMIN-AUTHORIZED-USE-D01] User need: `authenticate a named user` through `POST /auth/login`; actor=`admin`; RBAC scope=`public`.
[PRD-R01-ADMIN-AUTHORIZED-USE-D02] Scenario procedure: Submit a valid request body and valid session; for a 202 response follow the returned job/environment identifier until observed state is known. Apply to `POST /auth/login` as `ADMIN` at `public` scope.
[PRD-R01-ADMIN-AUTHORIZED-USE-D03] Required product behavior: Valid public input returns the documented result; public access grants no access to unrelated authenticated resources.
[PRD-R01-ADMIN-AUTHORIZED-USE-D04] Evidence: T-RBAC-01 must assert `R01/ADMIN/AUTHORIZED-USE`; T-AUTH-01, T-AUTH-02, T-AUTH-03 checks `authenticate a named user` here. Expected product result: Required product behavior: Valid public input returns the documented result; public access grants no access to unrelated authenticated resources.
### PRD-R01-ADMIN-ROLE-DENIAL
[PRD-R01-ADMIN-ROLE-DENIAL-D01] User need: `authenticate a named user` through `POST /auth/login`; actor=`admin`; RBAC scope=`public`.
[PRD-R01-ADMIN-ROLE-DENIAL-D02] Scenario procedure: Sign in as a role excluded from this rule and call the exact path; verify denial occurs before any protected read or mutation. Apply to `POST /auth/login` as `ADMIN` at `public` scope.
[PRD-R01-ADMIN-ROLE-DENIAL-D03] Required product behavior: `admin` is listed for this rule; authorization proceeds to its scope and business checks, with no privilege beyond `public`.
